paper_title: The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking capabilities on frontier mathematical problems, it remains unclear whether they possess the structural mathematical understanding underlying their solutions. In this paper, we take a first step toward systematically studying mathematical understanding in LLMs, from diagnosing its distinct capabilities to leveraging these findings to improve post-training. First, we introduce the notion of Mathematical Primitive to probe structural mathematical understanding and propose \hlei{}, a novel benchmark that evaluates mathematical reasoning along four distinct dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Second, our systematic diagnosis shows that solution accuracy masks distinct capability profiles, primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and Discovery is the dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. Our post-training analysis further shows that discovery-limited failures are particularly amenable to repair. Finally, building on these findings, we introduce \abs{}, a primitive-privileged self-distillation framework that selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \abs{} consistently improves mathematical reasoning over baselines across model scales and challenging benchmarks.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have driven rapid progress in mathematical problem solving, with frontier models increasingly capable of tackling research-level questions and, in several recent cases, resolving or making substantive progress on long-standing open problems (OpenAI, 2026a;b; Claude, 2026; Bubeck et al., 2025; Jang & Ryu, 2025). Yet these striking successes leave unresolved more foundational question: what models actually understand about the problems they solve and the mathematical content of the solutions they produce. Successful problem solving does not necessarily imply such understanding: models may arrive at correct answers through specious deductions (Boye & Moell, 2025), while conversely identifying sound high-level proof structures yet failing in low-level technical execution (Lu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). Existing works provide limited insight into this disconnect, as mathematical reasoning is still assessed primarily through outcome-level metrics such as final-answer accuracy or formal proof verifiability, obscuring whether success reflects the discovery of the mathematical structure needed for solution or merely the successful execution of derivation. Understanding mathematical reasoning therefore requires more than verifying that derivation is correct; it requires exposing the ideas that organize the argumentwhy it works, which components are essential, and what can be generalized or reused. LLM-generated proofs grow in scale and complexity: lengthy chains of valid steps may establish correctness while leaving the underlying mathematical structure difficult to identify. Recent work has begun to emphasize precisely these aspects of mathematical reasoning, calling for representations that reveal the motivation, structure, and key ideas underlying an argument rather than only its final outcome (Frieder et al., 2024). In his ICM 2026 lecture, Terence Tao similarly highlighted the importance of making machine-generated mathematics conceptually digestible (Tao, 2026), warning that optimizing primarily for formal correctness risks producing an increasing volume of valid but opaque proofs without corresponding increase in mathematical understanding. For LLMs, this perspective shifts the focus from merely producing valid proofs to determining whether the structural knowledge organizing those proofs is actually accessible to the model. In this paper, we systematically study structural mathematical understanding in LLMs, as illustrated in Figure 1: the ability to identify the compact, load-bearing mathematical structure that explains why solution works, distinct from the procedural ability to generate the derivation itself. We operationalize this notion through the Mathematical Primitive, concise, non-procedural representation of the foundational idea organizing solution, and introduce PRIM, benchmark spanning four complementary dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Our diagnosis reveals that ❶ similar solving accuracy can mask markedly different capability profiles, ❷ correct primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and, most importantly, ❸ independent Discovery is the dominant bottleneck to mathematical reasoning. We further find that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to post-training, but existing methods can introduce regressions on problems the model already solves. Motivated by these findings, we introduce ABSORB, post-training paradigm that uses Mathematical Primitives as privileged information and bounded override mechanism to selectively transfer their guidance into the students reasoning process, enabling primitive-guided reasoning to be internalized without access to primitives at inference time. sections.content: Rather than viewing mathematical problem solving as sequence of steps, we separate structural mathematical understanding from procedural execution. We formalize the distinction through the

sections.title: 2.1 MATHEMATICAL PRIMITIVE
sections.content: A mathematical solution often begins before the first line of proof, when an opaque problem is recognized through the structure that makes it solvable. We term this load-bearing structural understanding the Mathematical Primitive (Definition 1). Unlike generic advice such as use induction or apply theorem, primitive identifies the structural property that makes such strategy applicable. It therefore serves as an intermediate reasoning object between problem understanding and procedural solution construction. Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive). For mathematical problem, primitive is the essential conceptual observation that reveals why the problem can be solved. It captures the latent mathematical structure shared by the problem and its solution, such as an invariant, theorem condition, representation, reduction, or reformulation. primitive should be concise, problem-specific, and explanatory: it must make clear what property is being exploited and how that property unlocks the solution. It is not routine calculation, piece of generic advice, or full proof.

sections.title: 2.2 FOUR DIMENSIONS OF MATHEMATICAL UNDERSTANDING
sections.content: Taking the mathematical primitive as the fundamental concept of structural understanding, we systematically decompose mathematical reasoning into four complementary dimensions. Let denote the input problem, the corresponding mathematical primitive, complete proof or solution, and π an LLM solver. The four dimensions are defined as follows: Discovery (π(x) ˆp) measures whether the model can independently identify the load-bearing mathematical primitive from the input problem alone. Generation (π(x) ˆy) evaluates whether the model can solve the problem directly under zeroshot CoT prompting, with performance measured by exact match on the final answer. Digestion (π(x, y) ˆp) instead provides the model with complete correct solution and asks it to extract the mathematical primitive underlying the derivation, measuring whether the model can identify the underlying structure once valid reasoning trajectory is exposed. Execution (π(x, p) ˆy) conditions the solver on the mathematical primitive and evaluates whether it can successfully solve the problem once the relevant structure is explicitly provided. Both Discovery and Digestion are evaluated using the scoring protocol introduced in 2.3.

sections.title: 2.3 THE PRIM BENCHMARK
sections.content: Data Curation. We build on Humanitys Last Exam (HLE) (Center for AI Safety et al., 2026), focusing on its mathematics, text-only, free-form subset with exactMatch evaluation. To reduce annotation noise in the original benchmark, we draw from the HLE-VERIFIED release (Zhai et al., 2026), retaining its Gold and Revision subsets, from which we randomly sample 200 problems. For each problem, GPT-5.4-High generates an initial primitive annotation conditioned on the problem, reference answer, and gold rationale, following Definition 1. Three human experts with graduate-level training in mathematics independently review the primitive and verify the validity of the problem, answer, and rationale. This process excludes 18 unsuitable problems, yielding final evaluation set of 182. Further curation and annotation details are provided in Appendix A.1. Primitive Scoring. We evaluate each predicted primitive against the human-annotated gold primitive, using the reference solution only to recognize mathematically equivalent formulations. To account for different forms of mathematical structure, each problem is assigned to one of three primitive families, including RECAST, WITNESS, and ARGUMENT, with full definitions provided in Appendix A.2. Our scoring rubric evaluates three aspects of predicted primitive: determines whether the response constitutes valid primitive, σgate measures whether it identifies the essential mathematical structure, and σmech measures whether it explains how that structure enables the solution. We define Score = σgate (cid:0)0.6 + 0.4 σmech (cid:1), PrimitiveAcc = 1 [Score τ ] , with τ = 0.8. This formulation treats validity and structural identification as necessary conditions, while using mechanism quality to refine the score. Further details are provided in Appendix A.3.

sections.title: 3 DIAGNOSING MATHEMATICAL REASONING
sections.content: In this section, we conduct an empirical study of diverse set of LLMs, including both openand closed-source models, on PRIM. Moving beyond standard answer correctness, our evaluation systematically disentangles procedural execution from structural understanding. We report model performance across four dimensions: Generation, Discovery, Digestion, and Execution, following the evaluation protocol described in 2.3. The main results are summarized in Table 1.

Finding 3: Independent structural discovery is the dominant bottleneck. As shown in Table 1, models perform substantially better on Digestion, recovering the Mathematical Primitive from correct solution, than on Discovery, where the same primitive must be identified from the problem alone. This asymmetry is particularly pronounced outside the strongest OpenAI models. Even models with weak Discovery can often recover the organizing primitive once the relevant reasoning is exposed through completed solution; for instance, Qwen3.6-27B rises from 24.73% Discovery to 92.31% Digestion and R1-Distill-32B from 6.04% to 65.38%. These results reveal pronounced gap between retrospective recognition and prospective discovery of mathematical structure: models can often recognize the key idea once it is instantiated in valid solution, yet struggle to identify it independently before the derivation is known. To further localize this bottleneck, we decompose Generation failures according to the joint outcomes of Discovery (D) and Execution (E), as shown in Figure 4. striking 83.6% of all failures fall into the regime, indicating that failed primitive discovery dominates the failure landscape. Importantly, substantial fraction of these cases are discoverylimited failures (DE+): the model fails to identify the correct primitive independently, yet succeeds once it is supplied. This reveals that, for many failures, latent execution capacity is already present but remains inaccessible because of the upstream bottleneck in primitive discovery.

While our preceding diagnosis reveals the failure modes of LLMs during inference, natural followup question arises: how does post-training impact these mathematical reasoning failures? Of particular interest are discovery-limited failures, which exhibit substantial room for improvement (3.2). We hypothesize that these failures lie just at the boundary of the models reasoning capabilities, making them highly amenable to repair through post-training. Therefore, we utilize Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) to investigate how different failure modes uniquely respond to these post-training paradigms. Our training corpus contains 709 Mathematics Ph.D. qualifying-examination problems from 19912026, each paired with human-authored proof (median length: 118 words); additional details are provided in Appendix C. We use qualifying-examination problems because their open-ended, proof-oriented nature closely matches the difficulty and structural reasoning demands of PRIM. sections.title: 4.1 PRIMITIVES AS PRIVILEGED INFORMATION
sections.content: Our diagnosis in 3 identifies missing mathematical primitives as the primary bottleneck in discoverylimited problems. natural remedy is to directly supervise primitive generation. In practice, however, this objective transfers poorly to solution reasoning, likely reflecting mismatch between structural understanding and step-by-step generation, as further supported by the ablations in Appendix E. More importantly, 3.3 shows that post-training can repair discovery-limited failures while leaving Discovery largely unchanged. This dissociation suggests that effective reasoning does not require primitives to be explicitly generated; instead, they can guide the reasoning trajectory implicitly. Figure 5: Illustration of ABSORB paradigm. Motivated by this observation, we provide mathematical primitives as privileged information to the teacher rather than as prediction targets for the student. This mirrors our Execution evaluation, where providing the primitive unlocks latent execution capability, and uses the same primitive-conditioned reasoning to guide post-training. Compared with full reference proofs, primitives provide more targeted supervision by supplying the missing structural information without prescribing execution steps the student can already perform. This design transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the students own generation process without requiring primitives at inference time.

sections.title: 4.2 BOUNDED OVERRIDE
sections.content: Given the reasoning drift observed with existing post-training methods, indiscriminate teacher intervention should be avoided. Moreover, introducing mathematical primitives as privileged information can cause substantial privilege leakage under naive OPSD on complex reasoning problems, as shown in Appendix E. This motivates selective transfer mechanism that preserves useful privileged guidance while limiting how strongly it can override the students own reasoning. Intuitively, the teacher should pull the student toward better choices without abruptly displacing preferences that the student has already formed. The primitive should refine the students existing reasoning space rather than force it to imitate decisions that are only accessible under privileged context. This leads to two design principles: ❶ when the privileged teacher assigns higher preference to choice than the student, this positive guidance should be transferred in full, as it directly reflects

sections.title: 4.4 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: Setup. For implementing ABSORB, we utilize the identical base models and optimization configurations detailed in 3.3, differing only in the substitution of the standard OPSD objective with our primitive-privileged divergence loss (LABSORB). To comprehensively evaluate internalized reasoning capabilities and generalization, we assess performance across four challenging mathematical benchmarks: our curated PRIM (evaluating both Generation and Discovery), the full mathematics subset of HLE-Verified (Zhai et al., 2026), HMMT25 (Dekoninck et al., 2026), and Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2025). To account for the extreme difficulty of the competition-level datasets, we report pass@4 accuracy for HMMT25 and Omni-MATH. The overall average (Avg.) is computed exclusively over the Generation scores across all four benchmarks, excluding Discovery. Results. As shown in Table 4, ABSORB consistently outperforms SFT and OPSD across model scales and benchmarks. At the 9B scale, SFT and OPSD reduce Generation accuracy by 6.04 and 4.95 percentage points, respectively, while OPSD incurs 3.30-point drop at the 27B scale. These regressions explain the modest net gains discussed in 3.3: repairing previously failed problems can be offset

sections.content: by newly introduced errors on problems the model already solves. In contrast, ABSORB improves Generation at all three model scales, including 5.49 point gain at 9B and 3.73 point improvement in average benchmark performance. This pattern is consistent with the role of bounded override: selective transfer retains useful primitive-guided information while limiting disruptive changes to the models existing reasoning behavior. The results also support the intended internalization of primitive-guided reasoning. Improvements from ABSORB are concentrated in downstream reasoning rather than explicit Discovery. At the 9B scale, Generation improves by 5.49 points while Discovery increases by only 1.10; at 27B, Generation improves by 1.10 points and HLE Math by 3.93, despite 0.55-point decrease in Discovery. Thus, the benefit of the primitive need not manifest as better explicit primitive recovery; instead, its structural guidance is increasingly reflected in the models unassisted reasoning process.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs. Mathematical reasoning benchmarks have rapidly escalated in difficulty, progressing from early grade-school and competition datasets (e.g., MathQA (Amini et al., 2019), ASDiv (Miao et al., 2020), SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021)) to advanced Olympiadand expert-level frontiers (TheoremQA (Chen et al., 2023), MathBench (Liu et al., 2024), AIME (Dekoninck et al., 2026), OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), Omni-MATH (Gao et al., 2025), HLE (Center for AI Safety et al., 2026), FrontierMath (Glazer et al., 2024)). Despite this scaling in complexity, evaluation predominantly remains rigidly anchored to final-answer correctness. Recognizing the limitations of outcome-based metrics, recent literature explores process-oriented evaluation: SMART (Hou et al., 2026) decomposes problem-solving across cognitive dimensions, ReasoningMath-Plus (Zheng et al., 2026) verifies minimal procedural skeletons, and DeepInsightTheorem (Li et al., 2026a) leverages proof sketches for intermediate supervision. Executable Functional Abstractions (EFAs) (Khan et al., 2025) represent mathematical structure as executable generative programs, whereas our Mathematical Primitive captures the concise, non-procedural idea underlying specific solution. Our approach instead isolates the load-bearing mathematical primitive, decoupling structural understanding from procedural execution. We evaluate whether models can discover it from problem, recover it from solution, and execute the proof when it is provided. On-Policy Self-Distillation. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) advances knowledge distillation for LLM reasoning by mitigating the distribution shift inherent in traditional off-policy methods (Zhao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Penaloza et al., 2026). Specifically, the student generates its own reasoning trajectories on-policy, while the teacher, conditioned on additional privileged information, provides dense supervision along these rollouts, with both sharing the same base model. However, recent studies show that naive OPSD can suffer from privilege leakage and suppress exploratory or selfcorrective reasoning. To address this, Shen et al. (2026) isolate inference-transferable supervision from reference-induced shortcuts, while Kaur et al. (2026); Peng et al. (2026) focus on preserving high-entropy decision points and epistemic behaviors from aggressive privileged-teacher corrections. Other approaches modulate supervision based on teacherstudent disagreement (Li et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026), or utilize RL primarily for token-level credit assignment (Yang et al., 2026). AVSD mitigates privilege leakage by separating shared and view-specific signals across multiple privileged views (Nguyen et al., 2026). ABSORB differs primarily in the privileged signal itself. Rather than conditioning the teacher on full solution, ABSORB uses the primitive as privileged information and selectively transfers its guidance through bounded override mechanism.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we introduced the notion of Mathematical Primitive and PRIM, benchmark for systematically evaluating structural mathematical understanding in LLMs across Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. Our diagnosis reveals that similar solution accuracy can mask markedly different capability profiles, correct primitives can unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and independent Discovery constitutes dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. We further show that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to post-training, while existing methods can introduce regressions on problems the model already solves. Building on these findings, we

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: proposed ABSORB, primitive-privileged post-training paradigm that selectively transfers primitiveguided reasoning through bounded override mechanism. Experiments on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that ABSORB consistently improves over strong post-training baselines. Overall, our results highlight the value of explicitly diagnosing structural mathematical understanding and leveraging this structure to improve LLM reasoning. By systematically investigating mathematical understanding in LLMs, we hope this work encourages broader shift in AI for Science from optimizing benchmark performance alone toward identifying the capabilities required for scientific problem solving and discovery. Given the foundational role of mathematics across STEM disciplines, this structural perspective may extend beyond mathematics. We highlight three promising directions. First, our diagnostic framework could be generalized to other structurally rigorous domains, such as theoretical physics and computational chemistry. Second, the observed discovery-execution asymmetry suggests potential design principle for mathematical agents: explicitly separating structural search from procedural execution may enable more effective allocation of inference-time computation. Finally, future work could explore integrating mathematical primitives with formal verification systems such as Lean, connecting informal structural reasoning with formal proof generation.

sections.title: A DATA CURATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 DATASET FILTERING AND CORRECTION To reduce annotation noise in the original HLE, we draw from the community-verified HLEVERIFIED release (Zhai et al., 2026), retaining only its Gold and Revision subsets. We randomly sample 200 text-only problems and conduct an additional expert review for primitive-level evaluation. This process excludes 18 unsuitable problems due to ill-posed or ambiguous questions, incorrect or unverifiable answers, non-self-contained tasks, insufficient rationales, exhaustive-computation requirements, or other quality issues. For 17 of these 18 problems, no valid gold primitive could be established, yielding final benchmark of 182 problems. Expert review further identifies residual errors in the official answers of 15 retained problems, including 13 mathematical errors and 2 corrupted answer strings, which we correct in our benchmark. Re-evaluating the strongest model on these corrected answers flips 11 predictions from incorrect to correct, with no reverse flips, providing an additional consistency check on the revisions. Because gold primitives are derived with access to reference solutions, we also audit them for answer leakage. We search the concatenated primitive fields for bounded occurrences of the gold answer, using token boundaries designed to avoid spurious numeral matches. This audit initially identifies 4 affected primitives. We manually revise them to remove the leaked answers while preserving their structural content, and verify that no direct answer-string leakage remains in the final benchmark. The rationale is provided only so the judge can recognize coarser phrasings, equivalent paraphrases, or alternative routes that the reference solution shows to be valid, i.e. so correct primitive is not penalized merely for failing to match the terse gold annotation verbatim, while never requiring the model to reproduce the downstream execution. sections.title: ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE OF MATHEMATICAL PRIMITIVES
sections.content: To make the notion of mathematical primitive concrete, we provide representative example in Figure 6. The full rationale contains the complete derivation needed to solve the problem, whereas the primitive isolates the underlying structural idea that makes the derivation possible. Due to space constraints, we show only the core_concept field in the figure. This example illustrates that primitive is not shortened proof, but compact representation of the key mathematical structure underlying the solution. A.5 PROMPT ON EXTRACTING MATHEMATICAL PRIMITIVE AND PRIMITIVE SCORING During data curation, we use teacher model to extract mathematical primitive for each problem. As shown in Figure 7, the teacher is asked to identify the essential mathematical property underlying the problem and explain the solution principle enabled by that property, while explicitly avoiding calculations or solution steps. We additionally require structured primitive classification, including primary type, optional secondary types, classification rationale, and confidence score. We evaluate each predicted primitive using three complementary signals. First, the validity term checks whether the prediction contains substantive mathematical primitive rather than vacuous response, such as generic advice, bare technique name, or computation without conceptual claim (Figure 8). For predictions that pass this check, we separately assess the correctness of the GATE and MECHANISM components using the reference solution and gold primitive (Figure 9). The GATE score σgate measures whether the prediction identifies the essential problem-specific idea, the what that unlocks the problem, while the MECHANISM score σmech measures whether it correctly explains the high-level how, namely why that idea enables valid solution principle. Both correctness judgments emphasize semantic agreement rather than exact reproduction and do not penalize missing downstream execution details.

sections.content: Dual-channel is an alternative design motivated by our analysis of rescued trajectories, which suggested that primitive guidance primarily acts through early route selection and later adjudication. The route channel applies reverse KL only to the first 512 completion tokens. The adjudication channel operates at student-generated self-doubt forks (e.g., Wait, But, However, Actually) and asks the student to sample candidate continuations. The primitive-conditioned teacher provides only preference over these student-generated candidates rather than generating tokens itself. Given teacher and frozen-base scores zT and z0, we form the base-corrected teacher preference qT = softmax (cid:18) zT z0 0.2 (cid:19) , and optimize Ladj = DKL(qT qS), with weight 0.3 in addition to the early-route reverse-KL term. Because this variant uses larger 1,692problem pool, full-length primitive annotations, and 8k-token completions, it should be interpreted as reference alternative rather than strict single-variable ablation. It nevertheless substantially underperforms both the base model and ABSORB. We separately compare direct supervised objectives. Solution SFT fine-tunes the model on the human-authored reference solutions, while primitive SFT directly trains the model to generate the mathematical primitive. Solution SFT lowers Generation to 32.42, and primitive SFT performs worst overall, reducing Generation and Discovery to 28.02 and 2.75, respectively. Together, these results show that neither alternative teacher-guided distillation nor direct supervision on solutions or primitives substitutes for the combination used by ABSORB: primitive-conditioned teacher guidance transferred through bounded override while the student remains in solution-generation space. Teacher-guided distillation baselines include TOP-D (Xie et al., 2026) and our dual-channel alternative, while the SFT baselines directly supervise either the reference solution or the mathematical primitive. Dualchannel uses larger 1,692-problem training pool, full-length primitive annotations, and 8k-token completions, and is therefore included as reference alternative rather than strict single-variable ablation.
